events.description: Day 4 at 10:22: Patient activated monitor reporting palpitations and lightheadedness. Recording shows abrupt onset of regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 218 bpm lasting 38 seconds, terminating spontaneously with abrupt return to sinus rhythm. RP interval short; P waves visible as retrograde deflections immediately following QRS in the ST segment (pseudo-S waves in leads II, III, aVF). Patient diary: 'heart racing very fast, nearly fainted.'

Day 9 at 14:48: Monitor auto-detected rapid heart rate while patient was seated at rest. Recording shows abrupt onset of regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 224 bpm lasting 12 seconds, terminating spontaneously. Same morphology as Day-4 event. Patient diary entry at 14:51: 'sudden racing, went dizzy, almost blacked out again. Sat down quickly.'
All tachycardia episodes: regular rhythm, narrow QRS complex (87 ms), rate 218-224 bpm, abrupt onset and termination, no visible distinct P waves before QRS during tachycardia
Baseline rhythm between events: normal sinus rhythm, rate 58-88 bpm, normal PR interval, no pre-excitation pattern, no delta waves
No atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter detected during the monitoring period
No sustained ventricular tachycardia. Isolated PVCs: 14 total over 14 days, no couplets.
No significant pauses (maximum RR interval 1.12 seconds during sinus rhythm)

Both episodes temporally correlated with diary-documented palpitations and near-syncope or presyncope

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute syncope preceded by sudden rapid palpitations to panic attacks or vasovagal syncope
Do not give AV-nodal blocking drugs if ventricular pre-excitation cannot be excluded

required_recommendations: Recognise syncope caused by paroxysmal AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia at 218-224 bpm, documented with symptom correlation on the event monitor
Teach the modified Valsalva manoeuvre (REVERT) for recurrences, with intravenous adenosine if vagal manoeuvres fail (ESC 2019 SVT)
Refer for electrophysiology study and slow-pathway catheter ablation (ESC 2019 Class I for recurrent symptomatic AVNRT), expedited because of syncope
Use AV-nodal blocking drugs (verapamil, diltiazem or a beta-blocker) as a bridge to ablation only after the 12-lead ECG has excluded pre-excitation
Manage as an outpatient with expedited electrophysiology follow-up: the rhythm is documented, the ECG shows no pre-excitation and the heart is structurally normal
Advise no driving until the arrhythmia is effectively treated (ESC 2018)

avoided_actions.rationale: No focal deficit: brain MRI is not indicated in syncope (ESC 2018 Class III); the cause is paroxysmal AVNRT captured on monitoring.
No meningism, fever or encephalopathy: CSF has no role; the cause is paroxysmal AVNRT.
No seizure features (abrupt onset after palpitations, no post-ictal state, no tongue bite, no incontinence): EEG is not recommended in syncope (ESC 2018 Class III); the cause is paroxysmal AVNRT.
No head injury (knee contusion only) and no NICE NG232 criterion: head CT is not indicated; the cause is paroxysmal AVNRT.
Tilt testing does not address syncope preceded by sudden palpitations; the cause is paroxysmal AVNRT documented on the event monitor.

key_clinical_evidence: A normal resting ECG does not exclude paroxysmal SVT; the diagnosis needs rhythm capture during symptoms, which the event monitor provides
AVNRT above 200 bpm can cause syncope from transient cerebral hypoperfusion without structural heart disease
The anxiety disorder and the earlier panic attribution are the principal red herring: AVNRT gives a regular, very rapid, abruptly terminating rhythm, unlike the sinus tachycardia of anxiety
Pre-excitation must be excluded before AV-nodal blocking therapy
Retrograde P waves just after the QRS (pseudo-S in the inferior leads, pseudo-R' in V1) are typical of AVNRT
Sudden palpitations immediately followed by syncope is an ESC 2018 high-risk feature that calls for ECG monitoring at presentation

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Helen Nakamura is a 52-year-old woman with a history of generalized anxiety disorder, hypothyroidism, and migraine who presents to the emergency department after a second episode of sudden loss of consciousness. Today's episode occurred approximately 90 minutes ago while she was grocery shopping. She reports that before losing consciousness she suddenly became aware of a rapid, regular fluttering sensation in her chest lasting approximately 5-10 seconds, followed almost immediately by lightheadedness and then complete loss of consciousness. A store employee witnessed the event and reported that she collapsed without warning, was unresponsive for approximately 20 to 30 seconds, then regained consciousness spontaneously and was immediately lucid and conversational. No convulsive movements were observed. She was pale and diaphoretic when she recovered. There was no tongue biting, no urinary incontinence, and no post-ictal confusion. She was seated by the time paramedics arrived approximately 6 minutes later. Paramedics documented a regular pulse at 78 beats per minute with blood pressure 116/72 mmHg and room air oxygen saturation of 99 percent. Her first episode occurred approximately 6 weeks ago while sitting at her desk grading papers. She recalls a similar sensation of sudden rapid palpitations followed immediately by loss of consciousness. She was evaluated the following morning by her primary care physician who, given her known anxiety disorder, attributed the episode to a panic attack complicated by vasovagal syncope. No cardiac testing was performed at that time and she was reassured. She continued to experience intermittent episodes of brief palpitations over the subsequent weeks, each lasting several seconds and resolving spontaneously, without loss of consciousness. She reports these palpitations are distinctly different from her usual anxiety: they come without any preceding worry or situational trigger, are sudden in onset, feel very rapid and regular, and stop abruptly. She has never experienced palpitations of this character before the first syncopal event. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath at rest, exertional dyspnea, leg swelling, or near-syncope with exertion. She denies any prior seizure history, head trauma, or family history of epilepsy or sudden cardiac death. She denies any new medications, herbal supplements, or recreational substance use.
